content: The cost-effectiveness of the test can favor the intervention, the comparison, neither, or vary depending on the setting. In some cases, no studies are included to determine this. The impact of the test on health equity can be reduced, increased, variable, or unknown. The acceptability of the test to key stakeholders can be positive, negative, variable, or unknown. This depends on the setting and the availability of chest X-rays (CXR). The feasibility of implementing the test can be positive, negative, variable, or unknown. This depends on the setting, the availability of CXR, and human resources. The accuracy of symptomatic screening and/or CXR to exclude tuberculosis (TB) disease in contacts of people with pulmonary TB without HIV in high TB incidence countries varies. The absence of symptoms and abnormal CXR findings can be used to rule out active TB disease among HIV-negative household contacts aged ≥5 years and other at-risk groups before preventive treatment. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. The potential benefits of screening for active TB using a combination of any CXR abnormality and TB symptoms outweigh the harms. This screening rule is reliable for excluding active TB before providing preventive treatment. Symptom screening, with or without the addition of abnormal CXR, is acceptable to individuals and program managers. The use of CXR can enhance healthcare providers' confidence in ruling out active TB and reduce concerns about drug resistance development. However, adding CXR may increase costs and inconvenience for clients, as more individuals will undergo investigations for TB and other diseases. Contacts with abnormal CXR findings or TB symptoms must be properly followed up and investigated for TB and other diseases. Investigations should align with national guidelines and sound clinical practice. Contacts in whom active TB is excluded after investigations can be considered for preventive treatment. Radiologists and other resources must be available to implement the screening rule. Where CXR is unavailable, contacts should be screened for any TB symptoms, offering the highest sensitivity among symptom screening rules with high negative predictive value in most settings. Monitoring and evaluation should focus on the accuracy and feasibility of the recommended screening algorithm under programmatic conditions. Research priorities include household models to improve intervention delivery effectiveness and efficiency, and studies on the cost-effectiveness of screening rules, such as the use of mobile CXR. The accuracy of symptomatic screening and/or CXR to exclude TB disease in contacts of people with pulmonary TB without HIV in high TB incidence countries has been assessed. The index test is any abnormality in CXR, and the reference test is sputum culture and/or smear. Testing occurs at triage, with a pathway involving CXR positivity leading to confirmatory tests (mycobacterial culture or GeneXpert) and anti-TB chemotherapy (6–9 months of antibiotics). The quality of evidence is moderate for true positives and true negatives, with some limitations in study design, indirectness, and inconsistency. Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) could be used as an alternative to tuberculin skin tests (TSTs) to identify individuals at the highest risk of progression from latent TB infection (LTBI) to active TB in high TB incidence settings. There is no gold standard for LTBI diagnosis. TST and IGRA indirectly identify TB infection by detecting memory T-cell responses to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens. Both are acceptable but imperfect tests. WHO currently recommends that IGRA should not replace TST in high TB incidence countries due to similar performance in predicting active TB development, high cost, and technical complexity. Either IGRA or TST can be used for LTBI testing in high-income and upper-middle-income countries with an estimated TB incidence <100 per 100,000. The global shortage of purified protein derivative for TST has created barriers to scaling up LTBI management, and IGRA availability may facilitate this process. The performance of LTBI tests is better assessed by their predictive utility for active TB development. The primary effect measure of interest is the relative risk ratio for TB among test-positives and test-negatives, compared for TST and IGRA. The main outcome is the incidence of active TB in high TB incidence countries (≥100 per 100,000 population). The perspective is from the health system and public health. The balance of effects between IGRA and TST in high TB incidence countries has been studied. Five relevant prospective cohort studies (N = 7769) were identified, conducted in India and South Africa, involving populations such as people living with HIV (PLHIV), pregnant women, adolescents, healthcare workers, and household contacts. The pooled effect estimates for IGRA were slightly higher, with lower heterogeneity than TST, but the confidence intervals overlapped and were imprecise. There was little evidence for specific at-risk populations, and pooled estimates for PLHIV were imprecise. The overall certainty of evidence for effects is low to very low. There is important uncertainty or variation in how much people value the main outcomes, with no evidence retrieved. Resource requirements for IGRA compared to TST vary. A systematic review of cost-effectiveness studies showed that IGRA is generally more cost-effective than TST in immunocompromised populations, but results depend on the assumed performance of the tests. In some cases, providing preventive treatment without testing is the most cost-effective approach.
